title: Ratnakara asks his family
hookLine: a robber asks his family to share his sin, and Patanjali's sutra on turning a harmful thought around
carry: see where harm ends, then cultivate its opposite
tomorrow: Who is Ishvara in the Yoga Sutra?

cards: Before he was the poet of the Ramayana, a well-loved later story says, Valmiki was a highway robber named Ratnakara. He stopped travelers in the forest and took what they had, to feed his family.
One day he stops a sage, Narada in many tellings, who isn't afraid. The sage asks one question. Your family eats from this.
Will they share the sin of it too? Go and ask. Ratnakara goes home and asks.
Every one of them says no. The food is ours. The deed is yours.

teach.b: Ratnakara follows his harm to where it ends, and it ends with him alone. So he turns. He sits chanting Rama's name so long, the story goes, that an anthill rises over him, valmika, and he comes out as Valmiki.
Patanjali puts that same turn into a sutra.

Just after the restraints, beginning with ahimsa, non-harm, and the observances, he says, in paraphrase: when thoughts that pull against these trouble you, cultivate the opposite. Pratipaksha bhavana.
The next sutra takes the harmful thought apart. It may be done by you, done through someone else, or just approved of.
It may come from greed, anger or confusion. It may be mild, middling or intense. Whichever it is, it ends in endless pain and not knowing.
Seeing that, cultivate the opposite. So this isn't, think happy thoughts.

teach.h: FOLLOW IT TO WHERE IT ENDS.
teach.b: You follow the thought honestly to where it leads, the way Ratnakara walked home and asked. Many teachers read the story that way.
Vyasa's commentary pictures someone tempted to harm remembering why they took up yoga at all. That's the week: a seed, a dancer, a prince, a serpent, a wind. Now a storm, and Yoga's answer.
Not fight it, not obey it. Turn it around.

how: In the Yoga Sutras, the counsel to cultivate the opposite sits right after the restraints, such as non-harm, and the observances; students of Yoga philosophy practice it in reflection and in the moment a harmful thought arises, and the robber who became Valmiki is a story Hindu families tell children about owning what you do.

o: pushing angry thoughts away until they disappear
turning a harmful thought around to its other side
repeating cheerful words until the mood lifts

games.q: how the sutra takes a harmful thought apart — tap the pairs.
p: by you, through others, or approved

s: pratipaksha bhavana means pushing bad thoughts away with happy ones
it starts by following the harmful thought to where it leads, and seeing its cost.
the sutra counts approving of harm alongside doing it
done, caused to be done, or approved: all three are on the list.
the advice to cultivate the opposite comes right after the restraints, like non-harm, and the observances
Patanjali sets it just after them, for the moments a list isn't enough.

games.q: you're Ratnakara. your family has just said the sin is yours alone. by Patanjali's sutra, what's the move?
o: back to the road; they still need feeding.
see where the deed ends, and turn to its opposite.
blame the family for living off it.
games.why: that's pratipaksha bhavana: follow the harmful path to its end, pain and not knowing, then cultivate the other side. Ratnakara turned so fully he became Valmiki.

practice: Bring to mind one small, recent irritation, nothing raw, and let the sharp thought arrive.
Without scolding it, follow it a few steps ahead, if I said it, then what, and notice the cost; then let its other side come up, patience, fairness or simple quiet, and rest there for a few breaths.
If you pray, you can hold the person you were annoyed with in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Yoga. In Patanjali's sutras, when a thought against non-harm arrives, yoga means seeing where it ends and cultivating its opposite, pratipaksha bhavana.

orig.note: Sanskrit: cultivating the opposite side; Patanjali's counsel when harmful thoughts arise.

carryVoice: Your line: see where harm ends, then cultivate its opposite. Ratnakara asked, and turned. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 2.33 (when troubled by contrary thoughts, cultivate the opposite)
Yoga Sutras 2.34 (harmful thoughts done, caused or approved; from greed, anger or delusion; mild, middling or intense; ending in endless pain and ignorance)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 2.33 (the practitioner tempted to harm recalls the refuge of yoga)

Ratnakara/Valmiki legend (the robber asks his family to share his sin; chanting Rama's name; the anthill), in later tellings, not in Valmiki's Ramayana itself: the Adhyatma Ramayana tells it with seven sages; popular retellings name him Ratnakara and the sage Narada
